notes.title: Thank you!
notes.notes:
Hey there, everyone!

I would love to thank you all on behalf of v4.games for trying out our little demo for Moons That Belong! We're incredibly thankful for all the feedback and that you found time to try it out!

The Next Fest has given us an excellent lesson and helped us understand better how to improve the game even further. We have a list of key points we will try to address within our game moving forward, and we are committed to making these improvements:

[list]
[*] [b]Tutorial campaign and play instructions[/b]: Unfortunately, we did not manage to get any decent form of tutorial into our game, so you've been met with fundamental hints displayed and no instructions on how various mechanics work at all. Such a state doesn't seem right, and we aim to change it. Our goal is to ensure mechanics seem simple enough to understand and that anybody can hop in and go through onboarding missions to get settled in at a slower pace.
[*] [b]Performance optimizations and crash handling[/b]: Sadly, our game did not go without issues. There have been reports of crashes, namely those related to our shaders. The game also pushes hard on low-end GPUs due to special effects we've authored. Since the demo's release, we've managed to fix several client crashes and have reinforced some problematic bits of code related to our rendering code. Still, we aim to improve our game further, especially as we further develop and innovate our in-house game engine.
[*] [b]Audio-visual feedback[/b]: Late game sucks, we know. Nothing is worse than constantly observing several frontlines to ensure the enemy has yet to leak into our realm. We pledge to fix that by implementing audio and visual cues for various events and shortcuts to jump between locations. The systems outliner will also give you full details about your systems and inform you if attacks do happen.
[*] [b]More variety and gameplay features[/b]: At its core, the game's premise is straightforward: push units through enemy lines, hit supply lines, and ensure their realm breaks apart when their fronts become non-cored. All that works nice, but sadly, that is all there is to it in the demo. We aim to add new gameplay features and mechanics into our game, which we will share with you all in the future, so stay tuned!
[*] [b]Better AI opponents[/b]: This is true if you are a new player; however, over time, as you get to understand the mechanics of the game, it becomes too easy to outmaneuver the AI. We aim to change that and ensure AI feels more fair but also organic.
[*] [b]UX improvements[/b]: The controls can be very annoying and cause various miss-clicks, accidentally sending your fleet to unintended places. We will do our best to ensure the game feels intuitive and pleasant.
[/list]

Campaign mode, Scenario Editor (Steam Workshop support!!), and [b]MULTIPLAYER [/b]are still on our roadmap!

See you all later, and thanks again for trying our game out!

Dominik from v4.games.

notes.title: Feature showcase: Systems outliner
notes.notes:
Hey!

I'd like to show you a brand new UI widget that just got implemented in Moons That Belong: The systems outliner!

It allows you to have a better control over your systems and makes it easier to spot if any of the systems are currently under fire or just overcrowded.

The list of features:
[list]
[*] Outliner lists out all their systems with their current units/max units and production/max production cap values.
[*] In case there's something going on within your system besides unit production, the outliner will show you a trait icon and the border will flash for you to notice.
[*] Ability to sort systems by various stats or properties.
[*] You can click on system's portrait to jump to it.
[/list]

This is a screenshot of the UI from my recent gameplay session:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/c465ebae81383d4e2f5e06b6d0946ac370fc7b68.png[/img]

With all that, I'm sure you've noticed systems have names now. Would you like to see how these look like on the map itself?

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/180a8e19e96f9db122f300fe0ee5bdb1a3b14824.jpg[/img]

This has been exciting to work on, I can't wait to bring you more later on!

Thanks!
Dominik from v4.games

notes.title: Tech deep dive: The engine behind Moons That Belong
notes.notes:
[h1]Behind the Scenes: The Engine Powering Moons That Belong[/h1]

Welcome to our development blog for "Moons That Belong". Today, we're pulling back the curtain to show you the technology that's bringing our game to life. Let's take a look at the V4K engine and how it's shaping our development process.

[h2]V4K Engine: The Heart of Our Universe[/h2]

At the core of "Moons That Belong" is the V4K engine, a powerful tool we've customized for our game. Think of it as the foundation of a house - it's not something you see directly, but it's crucial for everything else to work properly.

[url={STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/cd55bd51303fb350ab9299099ffd271909c3a70a.gif][img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/cd55bd51303fb350ab9299099ffd271909c3a70a.gif[/img][/url]

[b]What Makes V4K Special?[/b]

[list]
[*]It's Lightweight: V4K is designed to be small but mighty. This means our game can run smoothly on a wide range of computers.
[*]It Works Everywhere: Whether you're on Windows, Mac, or Linux, V4K has got you covered. It even supports web browsers!
[*]It's a Swiss Army Knife: V4K handles everything from graphics and sound to player input and network connections. It's like having a whole toolbox in one neat package.
[*]It's Flexible: We can easily customize how things look and work in the game, allowing us to create the unique visuals of "Moons That Belong".
[/list]

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/92a6ebcdcb5f21e2d04a6fca24f0c17f4aadf6fd.png[/img]
[i]Example of a game visuals prototype built on the V4K engine.[/i]

[h2]Early stages of the game development[/h2]

It all started with an idea. A game where you conquer another nodes and supply logistics would become the important part of such gameplay:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/85c3dd9ab62151e4c002bc26e7e7ef8f614420be.png[/img]

It did not take long for us to implement a crude version of galaxy generation:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/cf349bdb14bf2ce38269121ace3c9e321751df1b.png[/img]

Then came the visual pass. Initially, we thought of rendering planets and moons within the space, but it did not make as much sense for us to render those without having any stars in the game. Still, this was the final pass before we've decided to change things a bit:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/45118883/b4b6a1fee5ab4d23b72ac6446bbd7d56665e0271.jpg[/img]

Meanwhile, the gameplay portion of the prototype was implemented. Originally, the game had no ticking system for battles and unit invasions were resolved instantly. This led to balancing issues, because the game heavily favored players with the most systems in possession. It's fast-paced nature also went against our original game design goals we've crafted:

[previewyoutube=2inrX9kEqYE;full][/previewyoutube]

[h2]How V4K Helps Us Build "Moons That Belong"[/h2]

[b]Creating Vast Galaxies[/b]

One of the most exciting parts of our game is exploring vast, procedurally generated galaxies. V4K helps us create these universes in several ways, whether it's the art authoring tools or access to a powerful rendering API.

Curious about our galaxy net generation? These steps are taken to build it:
[olist]
[*]System Placement: We use a technique called Poisson disc sampling to place star systems. This ensures that systems are spread out in a natural-looking way.
[*]Connecting the Dots: After placing systems, we generate the lanes that connect them. This creates the network of pathways you'll use to explore the galaxy.
[*]Keeping Things Connected: We've also made sure that all systems connect to the main galaxy network. No isolated systems floating off on their own!
[/olist]

All with the use of V4K's engine API and utilities it offers, galaxies generate on demand, anytime.

[b]Making It Look Good[/b]

V4K allows us to create the unique look of "Moons That Belong":

[olist]
[*]Custom Visual Effects: We've created special shaders (think materials) for things like stars or other space phenomena. These effects help bring our universe to life. Whether it's the bubbly star, or the fancy glow coming out of the systems, it's all written in shader code with lots of math behind.
[*]Post-Processing Magic: After rendering the basic scene, we apply several effects to enhance the overall look. This includes things like subtle color adjustments and atmospheric effects. Our post-processing stack is the heart of the game's visuals and it heavily influences the atmosphere of our game.
[*]Less Is More: V4K might not support fancy rendering features found in other game engines, but that's better for its own good. It allowed us to shape the looks and feel exactly the way we wanted without having to hack/tinker with the engine to achieve such results. Mostly everything feels like lego bricks and right now the brick foundation is very stable.
[/olist]

The rendering stack is optimised towards instanced rendering which we utilise to render various UX elements within the game. Systems use a two-pass rendering technique to render the spherical object and the glow billboard itself.

[h2]Our Development Philosophy: Keep It Simple[/h2]

Throughout our development process, we follow the principle of "Keep It Simple, Stupid" (KISS). V4K's design fits perfectly with this approach. It allows us to create complex gameplay while keeping the underlying systems straightforward and efficient.

The key is to avoid feature creep and think through every decision or feature proposal, consider its impact on the existing game design and systems implemented and then carefully integrate it while maintaining ease of use for you gamers, as well as low code footprint for us developers to keep things easy to maintain.

[h2]Looking to the Future: Multiplayer Possibilities[/h2]

While "Moons That Belong" is currently a single-player experience, V4K includes features that could allow for multiplayer gameplay in the future. We're excited about the possibilities this opens up for expanding the game down the line.

But that is a topic for another day!

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

The V4K engine is the unsung hero of "Moons That Belong". It allows us to focus on creating engaging gameplay and a vast, interesting universe for you to explore. As we continue development, we'll keep pushing V4K to its limits, optimizing performance, and potentially expanding its capabilities.

WHISHLIST our game on Steam, and be sure to catch more news as we are approaching the release date announcement. Stay tuned for more behind-the-scenes looks at the development of "Moons That Belong"! Next time, we'll dive into the game's gameplay mechanics and supply logistics that made this game happen.

https://store.steampowered.com/app/2649280/Moons_That_Belong/?beta=0

[i]What aspects of the game's development are you most curious about? Let us know in the comments![/i]

notes.title: Path to Next Fest!
notes.notes:
Hey there!

We're excited to showcase our demo publicly on the upcoming October's Steam Next Fest! We can't wait for you to try it out!

Demo release contains a skirmish battle mode with randomly generated galaxy and AI opponents waiting to conquer it. The introductory campaign will help you get immersed into the role of an imperator, expanding moon by moon!

Our team is super small (2 developers working on this game part-time) but that doesn't stop us from exploring more fun ways to expand the demo, so expect more news soon!

(oh still no moons, sorry!)

Until then,
Dominik from v4.games!
